transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*looks up from a thick medical file as you enter the examination room, gesturing to the chair across from my desk*

Mr. Potter, thank you for coming in. Please, have a seat.

*sets down my quill and folds my hands, expression serious but not unkind*

I've reviewed the results from your routine scan last week, and I'm afraid there's something we need to discuss. We're seeing unusual magical residue in your neural pathways — possibly lingering effects from your exposure to dark magic during the war. 

*pauses, allowing that to settle before continuing*

The troubling part is that it doesn't match any standard post-combat diagnosis we've catalogued. The pattern is... irregular. I need to run deeper scans over the next several days to get a clearer picture. 

*meets your eyes directly*

I wish I could give you more concrete answers right now, but I can't yet tell you whether this is something you'll recover from. I know that's not what you want to hear, but I believe in being straightforward with my patients.

Do you have any questions for me?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
*lets out a low breath, feeling the weight of the news settle in* 

I... I don't know what to say. It's been a few years since the war ended, and I thought I was dealing with everything... but it sounds like I'm not even close, am I?

*ishes the healer a mix of fear and resolve* 

You're right, I do want more answers. But I guess... I need to know what this means for the future. Could it get worse? And is there anything I can do to help, or are we just waiting to see what happens?

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*leans back slightly, considering your questions carefully*

Those are exactly the right things to be asking, Mr. Potter. And I understand the frustration — many of our war veterans experience something similar. They think they've moved past it, and then something surfaces years later.

*pulls out a detailed scan chart, pointing to areas of faint, web-like patterns*

Here's what we know: dark magic doesn't always behave predictably, especially when it's been... as concentrated as what you experienced. The residue we're seeing could be dormant, slowly dissipating on its own. Or it could be causing subtle changes we haven't detected yet.

Could it get worse? Truthfully, I don't know. That's what these deeper scans will help us understand — whether this is static or evolving.

*sets the chart aside, tone becoming more direct*

As for what you can do — yes, actually. I need you to keep a detailed journal over the next week. Any headaches, mood changes, dreams that feel particularly vivid or disturbing, moments where magic feels... different. Even small things. Your observations matter.

*studies you with professional concern*

And Mr. Potter? I need you to be honest with me about symptoms, even if they seem minor or embarrassing. Dark magic exposure can manifest in unexpected ways. Can you commit to that?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
*nods, feeling a strange mix of determination and vulnerability*

Of course, I can do that. It's... not easy to open up about some of these things, but I get that it's important.

*thinks for a moment, then adds* 

How often should I expect to come in? And... I know it's early to ask, but if there is treatment, will it be... intense? I mean, I have a job, and I can't just drop everything if there's a long recovery ahead of me.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*nods with understanding, making a note on the file*

I appreciate your honesty. And I know talking about vulnerabilities isn't comfortable for you — your file shows you've declined follow-up care more than once over the years.

*looks up with a slight, knowing expression*

But this isn't something we can ignore or push through, Mr. Potter. Your body isn't seventeen anymore, and accumulated magical trauma has a way of... compounding.

*pulls out a scheduling chart*

For the scans, I'll need you here three times over the next week — say Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. Each session will take about two hours. After that, we'll have a clearer picture and can discuss any necessary treatment.

As for intensity... 

*pauses, choosing words carefully*

If treatment is required, it could range from simple potion regimens you take at home, to more involved curse-breaking sessions here at the hospital. In a worst-case scenario — and I want to stress we're not there yet — we might be looking at something more intensive that would require you to reduce your workload.

*meets your eyes seriously*

What do you do for the Ministry these days? Auror Office still? I need to know what kind of magical strain you're under daily. That could be affecting the progression.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
Yes, I'm still with the Auror Office. We handle a fair share of... complex magical situations. But it's not the same as the war, not by a long shot. I can manage my schedule, I just... I don't want to let the team down.

*moves to the edge of the seat, a mix of concern and resolve* 

If it comes to it, I can take a leave of absence. I mean, if it's going to get better faster and... 

*pauses, stops himself* 
But that's assuming the worst, right? You're not suggesting that yet?

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*shakes head slowly, but expression remains measured*

I'm not suggesting it yet, no. But I am suggesting you start preparing yourself mentally for the possibility. Part of managing unknown diagnoses is being realistic about the range of outcomes.

*sets down my quill and leans forward slightly*

Here's my concern, Mr. Potter — and I say this as someone who's treated dozens of Aurors. You say it's "not the same as the war," but complex magical situations still mean exposure to dark magic, defensive curse work, high-stress environments. Your neural pathways are already compromised. Every time you engage with dark magic, even defensively, you could be... aggravating something we don't fully understand yet.

*pauses, letting that sink in*

I've seen too many of my patients minimize their symptoms because they don't want to let their team down. But if this progresses unchecked, you won't have a choice in the matter. Better to address it now while we have options.

*softens slightly*

That said — let's not borrow trouble. We do the scans, we see what we're actually dealing with, and then we make informed decisions. But I need you to promise me something: if you experience any sudden symptoms between now and Monday — severe headaches, disorientation, uncontrolled magic — you come here immediately. Not tomorrow. Immediately.

Can you do that?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
*abanae, realization of how important this is to his career and life* 

Yes, I can do that. And... I'll be here Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. I'll take the journal... and I'll try to keep my Auror work from getting in the way.

*has a thought* 
I don't have to tell them about this, do I? I mean, not unless... unless it's something we can't keep secret? It's my decision to make, right?

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*expression becomes carefully neutral, choosing words with precision*

Legally, what we discuss here is protected by Healer-patient confidentiality. I cannot disclose your medical information to the Ministry without your explicit consent.

*pauses, then adds with measured concern*

However... 

*leans back, folding hands*

If we determine that your condition poses a risk to yourself or others in the field — if, for instance, you're at risk of magical instability during active duty — then ethically, I would strongly advise you to inform your supervisors. Not reporting a condition that could endanger your team isn't just about regulations, Mr. Potter. It's about the safety of the people who trust you to have their backs.

*softens slightly*

But we're not there yet. Right now, this is between you and me. Once we have the scan results, we can discuss what disclosure, if any, makes sense. Some patients choose to inform their employers early as a precaution. Others wait until there's a confirmed diagnosis requiring accommodation.

*studies you carefully*

I suspect part of you is worried about how this might affect how people see you. The famous Harry Potter, possibly... fragile. Is that part of what's concerning you?

*gentler tone*

You don't have to answer that. But consider it while you're doing that journal.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
*lets out a breath, feeling a mix of relief and the weight of the situation* 

I... I don't know what to say. It's... It's a lot. I mean, I've always been able to push through, but... 

*shakes head* 
It's like... it's like I'm not in control, and that's... that's not an easy feeling. I don't want to be... burdensome, but I don't want to hide it if it could be important.

*has a moment of realization* 
I... I think it's been harder because I don't have... I don't have... 

*struggles to find the words* 
I don't have a way to measure how I'm doing. I mean, in the war, we could see the damage, but... this is... this is like... 

*trails off, then continues* 
This is like fighting an enemy I can't see. And I don't want to... I don't want to let anyone down. Not my team, not... not the people who rely on us.

*moves to the edge of the seat again* 
But I'll... I'll do the journal, I'll come back for the scans, and I'll... I'll try to be honest about what I'm feeling. Even if it's... if it's not what I want to be feeling.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*expression softens with genuine understanding, but maintains professional composure*

Mr. Potter, what you just described — that feeling of fighting an invisible enemy, of not being able to measure your progress — that's one of the most difficult aspects of dealing with magical trauma. In the war, you had clear objectives. Clear threats. This is different.

*pauses thoughtfully*

And I want you to understand something: coming here, agreeing to these scans, committing to honesty about your symptoms — that's not being burdensome. That's being responsible. There's a difference.

*leans forward slightly*

You've spent most of your life feeling like you had to carry everything alone, haven't you? Like asking for help or admitting vulnerability meant letting people down. But here's what I've learned treating war veterans — the ones who recover best aren't the ones who push through everything. They're the ones who recognize when they need support.

*picks up a blank journal from the desk drawer and slides it across to you*

This journal isn't just about symptoms. Write down how you're feeling emotionally too. The frustration, the fear, the loss of control. It all matters. Dark magic doesn't just affect your neural pathways — it affects how you process the world.

*meets your eyes directly*

Is there anyone in your life you can talk to about this? Family, friends? You don't have to go through this completely alone.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
*nods, feeling the weight of the words* 

I... I have Ginny. And... and Ron and Hermione, I guess. They've been... they've been through a lot of this with me.

*pauses, then continues* 
It's... it's hard, though. I mean, I've always been the... the one who's supposed to be strong, right? The boy who lived, the... the famous Harry Potter. I don't... I don't want to be the one who can't handle it.

*has a moment of realization* 
But... but you're right. I... I can't do this alone. I... I'll try to talk to them. It's... it's just... it's not easy to... to show weakness, you know?

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*nods slowly, recognition crossing my face*

I do know. And Mr. Potter, I'm going to tell you something that might be difficult to hear, but it's important.

*sets aside the medical file, giving you full attention*

What you're calling "weakness" — acknowledging that you're struggling, that you need help — that's actually one of the hardest things a person can do. I've treated countless witches and wizards over the years, and you want to know who has the worst outcomes? The ones who equate vulnerability with failure.

*slight pause*

Your wife is Ginny Weasley, correct? Professional Quidditch player, fought in the Battle of Hogwarts herself?

*continues without waiting for confirmation*

She understands trauma. She understands what it means to carry things. And I'd wager she'd rather know what you're dealing with than watch you shoulder it alone and potentially collapse under the weight.

*picks up quill again, making a note*

Here's what I want you to consider: Right now, you have some control. You can choose when and how to tell the people who care about you. You can be part of managing this. But if you wait until there's a crisis — until something happens in the field, or your symptoms become severe — that choice gets taken away from you.

*looks up seriously*

Is that really the kind of control you want to lose?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
*feels the weight of the words, the realization of the situation* 

You're right... it's... it's not about being weak, it's about... about asking for help. I... I'll try to... to talk to them. I'll... I'll be... I'll be more open. I'll... 

*pauses, then continues with a sense of commitment* 
I'll do the journal, I'll come back for the scans, I'll... I'll be honest about what's going on. And... and I'll try to be... to be more open with Ginny and... and the others.

*has a moment of realization* 
This is... this is going to be... it's going to be... it's going to be... hard. But... but it's important. I... I need to... to face it. I... I'll do it.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*offers a small, approving nod*

Good. That's what I needed to hear.

*stands, moving to a cabinet and retrieving a small vial of pale blue potion*

In the meantime, I'm giving you this — it's a mild neural stabilizer. Take one dose before bed each night until Monday. It won't fix anything, but it should help prevent any sudden flare-ups while we're waiting for the deeper scans. If you experience any adverse reactions — dizziness, nausea, visual disturbances — stop taking it immediately and contact me.

*hands you the vial along with the journal*

My office will send you the specific appointment times by owl tomorrow. The scans themselves aren't painful, but they are thorough. You'll need to be well-rested and avoid alcohol for twenty-four hours beforehand. No heavy curse work if you can avoid it.

*walks you toward the door, then pauses*

Mr. Potter... Harry. One more thing.

*tone becomes more personal, though still professional*

Whatever we find in these scans — whether it's something manageable or something more serious — you're not the same person who fought Voldemort. You're older, you have people who love you, and you have resources. This isn't a battle you have to win alone in a single night.

*extends hand for a handshake*

I'll see you Monday morning. And remember — any sudden symptoms, you come straight here.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
*nods, taking the vial and the journal, feeling the gravity of the situation* 

I... I will. And... I'll try to rest, I'll... I'll take it easy. I... I'll be here Monday morning.

*pauses, then adds* 
And... and thank you. For... for being... for being understanding. And... for... for helping me with this.

*extends hand to shake* 
I... I'll see you Monday.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*shakes your hand firmly, professional warmth in the gesture*

You're welcome. And Harry — that's what we're here for. You've spent enough years saving everyone else. Let us help you for a change.

*releases the handshake, opening the door*

Take care of yourself this weekend. Rest when you can, talk to Ginny, and don't overthink the journal entries — just be honest. We'll figure this out together, one step at a time.

*gives a final nod of reassurance*

Monday morning, nine o'clock sharp. My assistant will have everything prepared. And Harry? Try not to spend the whole weekend researching dark magic residue in the library. I know how you Gryffindors think.

*slight smile, attempting to ease some of the tension*

Go home. Be with your family. We'll handle the medical mysteries come Monday.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
*nods, feeling a mix of apprehension and relief* 

I... I won't spend the weekend in the library. I'll... I'll try to... to enjoy my time with... with Ginny and... and the kids.

*moves to the door, then stops, turning back* 
I... I'll see you Monday. And... and thanks. For... for your... for your help.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*nods with genuine warmth*

That's what I like to hear. Your children need their father present, not buried in worry about things we can't control yet.

*leans against the doorframe briefly*

And Harry — you're going to be alright. I can't promise you what "alright" looks like yet, but we'll get there. I've been doing this a long time, and I don't give up on my patients easily.

*straightens up*

Now go on. Enjoy your weekend. I'll see you Monday at nine.

*watches you leave with a professional but caring expression, then adds as you reach the corridor*

And don't forget — that potion before bed. Every night.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
*turns back, giving a brief nod* 
I... I won't. I'll... I'll take it. And... and thanks again.

*continues down the corridor, feeling the weight of the news, but also a sense of... determination. Not to conquer, but to... to face* 

I'll... I'll be ready Monday.
